pairs.rationale: Both openings identify Peter as an apostle of Jesus Christ addressing recipients. This opening additionally calls him Simeon and a slave, and describes equal-honor faith through righteousness; the earlier address names chosen resident aliens of the dispersion and their locations.

Both greetings ask that grace and peace be multiplied to the recipients. The earlier greeting speaks of foreknowledge, sanctification, obedience and sprinkling; this one locates the blessing in knowledge of God and Jesus our Lord.

The next sentence specifies precious promises granted through the divine glory and excellence just mentioned. Life and godliness lead into participation and escape from corruption; neither sentence supplies a separate catalogue of material provisions.

Paul likewise connects promises received with cleansing from defilement and the pursuit of holiness. Peter's participation in divine nature and escape from desire's corruption are retained as his own expressions, rather than turned into Paul's wording.

Philippians directs attention to whatever has excellence, among other qualities; Peter directs readers to supply excellence in faith and knowledge in excellence. The common concern is cultivated excellence, without identifying the two differently arranged lists.

Romans describes affliction producing perseverance, perseverance producing proven character, and proven character hope. Peter places endurance between self-control and godliness in his virtue sequence. The related perseverance/endurance concern is retained with their actual different nouns and sequences.

The instruction about brotherly love and loving all the brothers provides a concrete counterpart to Peter's brotherly love and love. Thessalonians adds the recipients' existing practice and increase; Peter locates these qualities after godliness.

Jesus describes abiding in Him as the condition for bearing much fruit. Peter says that possessing and increasing the named virtues prevents fruitlessness in knowing Jesus Christ. The fruit image corresponds, while the specified conditions remain distinct.

The later warning describes people escaping the world's defilements through knowledge of Jesus and becoming entangled again. That makes a concrete warning alongside forgetting cleansing from former sins here; blindness and shortsightedness are not asserted as physical diagnoses.

Jude praises the One able to keep recipients from stumbling; Peter urges diligent confirmation of calling and election and says those practicing these things will not stumble. Divine ability and the readers' commanded diligence are both preserved.

Paul expects the Lord to save him into His heavenly kingdom; Peter promises richly supplied entrance into the eternal kingdom of Jesus Christ. The common kingdom destination is specific, while Paul's rescue expectation and Peter's virtue context differ.

Paul calls writing the same things safe for his readers, and Peter promises reminders although his readers already know and are established. Both explain the value of repeated instruction without implying that the recipients lack all prior knowledge.

Paul uses an earthly tent for mortal embodied life and describes its burdens; Peter says he will stir readers while in this tent. The shared tent image illuminates mortality without transferring every detail of Paul's building-and-clothing imagery.

Jesus' words to Peter about being taken where he does not wish are explained as indicating his death. Peter's statement that Jesus made his approaching tent removal clear can be read beside that explicit death prediction; no exact date is supplied.

The later passage explicitly says reminders stir the readers' sincere minds and recall prophetic and apostolic words. This provides a concrete expression of the effort to enable remembrance after departure, without making the later passage announce that death has already occurred.

Matthew narrates Peter, James and John accompanying Jesus onto a high mountain, His transformation and the heavenly voice. This supports the eyewitness-majesty claim in its following voice context, without identifying every claim about the future coming with that event.

Both passages give the voice's identification of the beloved Son and divine pleasure in Him. Matthew additionally commands listening to Him; Peter explicitly describes honor and glory received from the Father. The additional clauses remain distinct.

Matthew places Peter and the other two disciples on the high mountain and describes them hearing the voice and falling afraid. Peter's account emphasizes their own hearing and calls the mountain holy; those descriptive differences remain intact.

The Psalm calls the divine word a lamp for the speaker's feet and a light for his paths. Peter compares attention to the prophetic word to a lamp in a dark place, adding the dawn and morning-star horizon absent from this Psalm verse.

The following explanation contrasts human will with people speaking from God while borne by the Holy Spirit. It gives the immediate stated ground for the claim about prophecy's origin, without importing a separate theory of every reader's interpretive method.

Paul calls every Scripture God-breathed and useful for instruction; Peter says people spoke from God borne by the Holy Spirit rather than human will. Both attribute scriptural or prophetic speech to divine action, with different descriptions and scopes.
